summary: Conduct the Earth is a web jukebox that turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into music in real time. Pick a visualization and press Play: frames are analysed, colours are decoded back into data through each visualization's own colour bar, and simple, honest rules turn the numbers into an orchestral score. Warmer water rises in pitch, extremes bring in the brass, lightning becomes drums placed where it strikes. Nobody has to touch anything: the data conducts. But anyone can take the baton with keys, mouse, touch or by waving a phone. It is built first for blind and low-vision people (full keyboard control, spoken descriptions with real units such as "about 18.8 °C", sound landmarks), and it is ready for reuse today: a Chrome extension that makes NASA's own SVS pages playable, a one-line embed for any website, a kiosk mode for museums and schools, and WAV/MIDI/MP4 export.
details:
What it does: for 9 visualizations from the challenge resources (sea surface currents and temperature, night lights, GEOS aerosols, ISS lightning, DYAMOND CO₂, GEDI forest height, an atmospheric river, Perpetual Ocean 2, air quality), Conduct the Earth plays a live sonification synchronised with the video, explains how to listen, and shows a built-in fidelity check.

How it works: Frames → Analyser → Features → Translation → Musical intents → Music system → Notes → Ensemble → Sound. Each frame is reduced to 160×80 px and every pixel is decoded through the visualization's colour bar (measured from the SVS colour bar images, with physical units: °C, m, ppm), or through brightness for light-based data. We measure the mean, spread, extremes, change between frames, flashes, and 32 values from west to east. Translations are monotonic: more always sounds higher or more intense, never the opposite. Musical intents (contour, tension, density, dynamics, a melody line that sweeps the map west to east and pans in stereo) become notes through a pluggable music system (tuning + scale + harmony) with pitches stored as fractional MIDI, so equal temperament, just intonation and micro-tonal, raga- or gamelan-inspired scales all fit. All voices are synthesised (orchestra, raw data, lullaby), so the audio is free to reuse.

Autopilot and conductor: the data drives tempo, loudness and sections by default. A person can add tempo, dynamics, sections on/off and a longitude "spotlight" (keys A S D F G, arrows, mouse, or a phone used as a baton); they shape the performance but never change what the data says. After 45 s of rest the autopilot returns, which suits museum screens.

Is the data audible? Every visualization runs a reverse test: how strongly note pitch correlates with the value under the needle (83–100% across the 9 visualizations), how smooth the melody is, and how many flashes became drum hits.

Ready for the EIC: a precompute pipeline turns an SVS number into a small feature file and an MP4 with our optional soundtrack next to the untouched original. A Chrome extension adds an optional "Play as music" button to every NASA SVS visualization page, so NASA's own site can be heard today without any change on NASA's side (https://earth-orchestra.pages.dev/earth-orchestra-extension.zip). One line embeds it in any page; kiosk mode runs unattended; WAV and MIDI export lets composers orchestrate the data.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve: most Earth data is shared as pictures, which leaves out people who cannot see them. Conduct the Earth lets blind and low-vision people, museum visitors, students and musicians hear real NASA data, and lets anyone feel the difference between a calm ocean and a heat anomaly. We hope the EIC and science museums adopt it as an optional soundtrack for their screens, and that teachers use the conductor mode to make Earth science a shared, playful class activity.

Factors we considered: scientific honesty (monotonic rules, colour bars decoded back to real units, a measurable reverse test), accessibility (keyboard-first, screen-reader descriptions, sound landmarks, no reliance on colour), musicality (scales, harmonic progressions and orchestration instead of raw beeps), reusability (open code, synthesised audio free of third-party licences, no change needed on NASA's side), and child safety and privacy (no accounts, no data collection).

Tools: TypeScript, Vite, Tone.js, @tonejs/midi, ffmpeg, Playwright, Cloudflare Pages and Pages Functions. Code: https://github.com/tchief/jukebox/tree/submission

Submitted version: https://conduct-the-earth.pages.dev (frozen, branch submission). Ongoing development after the hackathon: https://main.conduct-the-earth.pages.dev — for museums and galleries who want to try it; please judge the submitted version.

Install it as an app (PWA) on a phone or museum tablet: open the site and choose “Add to Home screen”. On a phone it becomes a conductor’s baton: raise it for more of the orchestra, tilt it to move the spotlight, turn it like a dial for timbre, shake it for a full-orchestra hit, and hold a finger on the map for a fermata.
